content: Down syndrome is a genetic condition caused by the presence of an extra copy of all or part of chromosome 21, also known as trisomy 21. This additional genetic material leads to a wide range of medical consequences, which can vary significantly between individuals and may affect any organ system or bodily function. The management of Down syndrome involves anticipating and preventing potential complications, recognizing and addressing specific health issues, and supporting individuals and their families in coping with the condition. The most common features of Down syndrome include distinctive facial characteristics, intellectual disability, congenital heart defects, hearing impairments, short stature, and an increased risk of developing Alzheimer’s disease. Less common but serious conditions associated with Down syndrome include leukemia, immune system deficiencies, and epilepsy. Interestingly, individuals with Down syndrome have a lower risk of developing certain conditions such as most types of cancer, atherosclerosis, and diabetic retinopathy. The variability in symptoms is influenced by complex interactions between genetic and environmental factors, and it is not possible to predict the specific manifestations of the condition before birth. Some health issues, such as congenital heart defects, are present at birth, while others, like epilepsy, may develop later in life. Endocrinology and Hematology Individuals with Down syndrome are at an increased risk of thyroid dysfunction, particularly hypothyroidism, which affects approximately one-third of individuals with the condition. Hypothyroidism may be congenital, due to the absence of the thyroid gland at birth, or acquired, often as a result of autoimmune thyroiditis. Reproductive health is also affected; women with Down syndrome have reduced fertility and are more likely to experience complications such as miscarriage, preterm birth, and difficult labor. However, they can have children without the extra chromosome 21. In contrast, men with Down syndrome are almost universally infertile due to defects in sperm production. Hematologic malignancies, particularly leukemia, are more common in children with Down syndrome. The risk of acute lymphoblastic leukemia is at least 10 times higher, and the risk of the megakaryoblastic form of acute myelogenous leukemia is at least 50 times higher in individuals with Down syndrome compared to the general population. Transient leukemia, a rare condition in the general population, affects up to 20% of newborns with Down syndrome. Although transient leukemia is typically self-limiting and resolves within a few months, it can lead to other serious health issues. Interestingly, solid tumors are less common in individuals with Down syndrome, possibly due to the presence of additional tumor suppressor genes in the extra genetic material. Gastrointestinal and Growth Down syndrome is associated with an increased risk of Hirschsprung’s disease, a condition in which nerve cells controlling parts of the colon are absent, leading to severe constipation. Other congenital gastrointestinal anomalies, such as duodenal atresia, annular pancreas, and imperforate anus, are also more common in individuals with Down syndrome. Additionally, gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) and celiac disease are more prevalent in this population. Growth parameters, including height, weight, and head circumference, are typically smaller in children with Down syndrome compared to their peers. Adults with Down syndrome are generally shorter than average, with men having an average height of 5 feet 1 inch (157 cm) and women averaging 4 feet 9 inches (144 cm). Obesity becomes a more significant concern as individuals with Down syndrome age. Axial Skeleton Individuals with Down syndrome are at an increased risk of atlanto-axial instability, a condition characterized by excessive movement between the first and second cervical vertebrae, likely due to ligamentous laxity. Periodic cervical spine X-rays are recommended to screen for this abnormality, as it can lead to spinal cord compression and neurological symptoms. Neurology Neurological manifestations of Down syndrome are evident early in life. Infants often exhibit decreased muscle tone (hypotonia) and increased joint flexibility. Developmental delays in motor and language milestones, such as sitting, walking, and talking, are common. Intellectual disability becomes more apparent as children grow. Epilepsy is more prevalent in individuals with Down syndrome, and the risk of Alzheimer’s disease is significantly increased. Signs of Alzheimer’s disease may appear in 10-25% of individuals with Down syndrome before the age of 50, with prevalence rising to 50% in the sixth decade and up to 75% in the seventh decade. This increased risk of dementia contributes to the reduced life expectancy observed in individuals with Down syndrome. Ophthalmology and Otolaryngology Eye disorders are common in individuals with Down syndrome. Nearly half have strabismus, a condition in which the eyes do not move in unison. Refractive errors requiring corrective lenses are also frequent. Cataracts and glaucoma are more prevalent in this population. Hearing loss affects more than half of individuals with Down syndrome, often due to recurrent middle ear infections (otitis media) and other factors. Obstructive sleep apnea is also more common in this group. Prevention and Screening The American Academy of Pediatrics and other health organizations have developed guidelines for screening individuals with Down syndrome for specific health conditions. These recommendations aim to identify and prevent complications associated with the condition. Routine newborn, childhood, and adult screening and vaccination programs should also be followed. Birth Newborns with Down syndrome should undergo a thorough physical examination to identify common features of the condition. An evaluation of the red reflex can help detect congenital cataracts, and eye movement should be assessed for strabismus. Constipation may indicate Hirschsprung’s disease, and feeding difficulties should prompt nutritional education. An echocardiogram should be performed by a pediatric cardiologist to identify congenital heart defects. A complete blood count is necessary to screen for leukemia, and thyroid function should be tested. Hearing should be evaluated using brainstem auditory evoked response (BAER) testing. Early intervention programs should be initiated to support learning and development. Childhood and Adulthood Growth in children with Down syndrome should be monitored using specialized growth charts. Thyroid function should be tested at 6 months, 12 months, and annually thereafter. Hearing should be assessed at every visit, and formal vision evaluations should be conducted every two years. After the age of three, cervical spine X-rays should be performed to screen for atlanto-axial instability. Annual screening for obstructive sleep apnea is recommended as the child grows. Treatment Treatment for Down syndrome is tailored to the individual’s specific health issues. For example, congenital heart defects may require corrective surgery shortly after birth, while other health problems may require minimal or no intervention. Plastic Surgery Plastic surgery has been proposed as a means of reducing the facial features associated with Down syndrome to decrease social stigma and improve quality of life. However, this practice is controversial and uncommon. Studies have shown mixed results, with some parents reporting improvements in their child’s appearance and speech, but independent evaluators often finding no significant changes. The National Down Syndrome Society advocates for acceptance and inclusion based on individuality rather than appearance. Alternative Treatments Some organizations, such as the Institutes for the Achievement of Human Potential, promote alternative therapies like psychomotor patterning for children with Down syndrome. However, these approaches lack scientific evidence and are not widely accepted in the medical community. Lifespan Life expectancy for individuals with Down syndrome has increased significantly over the past century. In the United States, the average lifespan is now approximately 49 years, compared to 25 years in 1980 and just 10 years in 1929. Advances in medical care, particularly for congenital heart defects, leukemia, and hypothyroidism, have contributed to this improvement. However, neurodegenerative conditions like Alzheimer’s disease remain a significant factor limiting life expectancy, and it is unlikely that the average lifespan for individuals with Down syndrome will reach that of the general population.
